From Florence, after a «painful» journey, she asks her to send two Sisters.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. My journey, as usual, was painful, for I had a bad headache,1 so that on reaching home I threw myself on the bed in despair.

  2. Listen, as soon as you receive this, send the two sisters, Sr. A. Martina and Sr. A. Stanislaa, here at once; the fare from Pisa to Florence is F. 12.70 for the two.2

  3. Tell Fr Accinelli to buy me one of the cheap chalices and give it to the sisters you are to send. Be as quick as you can; at once, at once.

  4. For your guidance, when I leave I shall let you know two days beforehand.3 I hope those from Piacenza have reached you.4

Goodbye, in haste, your [...]; greet Accinelli for me, and believe me yours

Affect. M. R.

Willing to send the Sisters, she makes some remarks about their number and the service they are to give in the school and possibly in the hospital.1

[Dear Mr Mayor,]

  1. I have received your esteemed letter of 27 April. Before sending you the papers Your Lordship requests,2 allow me to make some observations about the said Sisters, which Your Lordship in your wisdom will surely approve.

  2. Having to send three sisters there on a stipend of 1,100 Lire, and not knowing for certain what the Comune3 will give them, this is too little.

  3. Moreover, as I cannot clearly make out from your esteemed letter whether these three Sisters are also to look after the Hospital, this could not possibly be accepted, because the three who teach cannot have duties other than those of the school itself.4

  4. Though sending you 3 at your expense, I would add one more at my own expense, providing them with their bed.

  5. As for the hospital, Your Lordship should know that we have not only the management but also the care and nursing of the sick themselves, doing all the menial work and the cooking; and so in the Hospitals entrusted to us we have only one attendant, who gives the men those services modesty does not allow us; for the rest...

  6. As for teachers, from what I gather from yours, one qualified teacher with a trainee assistant would suffice. Kindly reply as soon as possible,5 as I need to know how to arrange things, having many other requests for other houses. Confident of a kind reply, I sign myself with every esteem

Humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Intending to open an institution for the free education of deaf girls, she asks for suitable municipal premises to be made available.1

[Most Illustrious Councillors,]

  1. I, the undersigned, placing my trust in the kindness that inspires Your Most Illustrious Lordships, turn to you to obtain a favour that will benefit this city and Province.

  2. It is my intention to open a home2 for Deaf-mute girls, who will be taken in, maintained and educated free of charge; but to carry out this wish I need to find suitable premises, as I have none available for the purpose.

  3. I applied for it to the Honourable Municipal Board,3 to whom I also explained my intention, and was told to turn to Your Most Illustrious Lordships; this I now do, earnestly begging you to grant me free municipal premises for a free home for Deaf-mute girls, leaving it to your wisdom as regards both the education and the healthiness of the place.

  4. The benefit this work will bring, and above all the philanthropy of Your Most Illustrious Lordships, make me hope to obtain what I ask,4 and in this hope I remain

Your Most Illustrious Lordships'

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She will send her the «dialogue» as soon as possible. She encourages her to keep up her school work and explains how to manage in the summer.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received your little letter and hear what you say about the dialogue; I wrote at once to Onorata to write it and send it to me; as soon as I have it [...].1

  2. Take care of yourself; I hear what a celebration you had in Via Pettinari.2 See, Daughter, how sweet the Lord is! Surely He wants to be loved and served as He deserves.

  3. As for that wretched woman, don't worry, for the Lord knows well how to uncover things; unfortunately He will make her known and she will be put to shame;3 all too soon we see our misdeeds come to light; so courage!

  4. Listen, so as not to have to write again, for I have too much to do, I tell you now what I would like you to do when you have held the June examinations. At the end, as it will be very hot then and it is not wise to keep school, for otherwise you certainly will not hold out,4 it is better to do this: all those at the Fornaci will come to the Parrocchietta and you will go to Rome; then when the others come to Piacenza, if you are not well you will come too.5

  5. And Sr. A. Crocifissa can manage with the others; they can keep the girls occupied and meanwhile teach a little Christian doctrine.6 Do you think I am right? I believe so. Goodbye; I am your Affect. M., who wishes you a thousand blessings, and am

your affect. M. R.

She sets out the essential conditions for sending the Sisters.

Dear Mr Mayor,

  1. In reply to your esteemed letter of 8 May,1 the agreement is settled for 3 Sisters at 1,700 Lire a year, in addition to everything in the first request.2

  2. For the moment I send you the name of the Qualified Teacher, and that of the Assistant, as I do not have the diploma and other papers here in this house where I am passing through;3 but I shall write at once to have them sent to me, and as soon as I have them I shall forward them to Your Lordship.

Please accept my sentiments of deep esteem

Humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Travel paid and only one Diploma.

She advises sending an ailing Sister to Sestri for a change of air. She will go to Ferrara and then return to Piacenza.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received yours telling me that the newly-weds have arrived in Genoa;1 I wrote to them, addressing the letter to Mamma, that is, to the house in Scurreria.2 So you are truly everyone's refuge; surely they will have been glad to stay, being free to do as they thought best. A pity you are so cramped; if you could see how big it is here! You surely ought not to be so badly off.3

  2. Listen, that sister who was in such poor shape, you know, the one you told me was from Cortemaggiore and whose periods were irregular; I think you might send her to Sestri for a while to see whether she recovers.4 What do you say? Otherwise she will need a change of air while there is still time; write and tell me.5

  3. Listen, I had thought of leaving for Ferrara on Saturday,6 but address your letters to Piacenza, where I am giving orders for them all to be kept for me. And try to go to the blind girls again to see whether the little machines [are] there; otherwise I fear they will forget the little they know.7 Goodbye, dear Daughter; please have them pray, for I am in extreme need. Goodbye, your

Most affect. M. R.

She arranges the transfer of some Sisters. She asks her to buy and send twelve beds. A Sister will arrive from Piacenza bringing the ducks.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, if the sister recovers, keep her, as you say, the one from Cortemaggiore.1 On my orders you will go and fetch Sr. A. Graziosa, Sr. A. Chiara and Sr. A. Federica from the S. P. D'Arena hospital; you will take there the two I sent you last, who were still here, that is, the ones sent, whom I had brought from Piacenza.2 Do you understand? See that you do at once what I tell you.

2. Now I would ask you another big favour: to have twelve iron beds sent to me like yours, with the curtains, that is, the rods for hanging curtains; in short, like the ones you have. Listen, I shall pay you for them little by little; take your time, a year or at least six months; what do you say? But I would like them soon, as soon as possible.3

3. For the rest, I hear that all is going well, and I bless God for it; I shall send you a Sister whom you will send on to the hospital. She will bring you some ducks: 12 are for Mamma,4 and you will take them to her at once; the others are for you. Take them to Mamma at once.

4. So you need no permission to go and see her, because whenever she wishes you may go, and with whomever she wishes. Goodbye, your; tell Fr Accinelli to write to me at once whether he has received my letter dated today. Many greetings to the sisters, and believe me your affect.

M. R.

She arranges for a Sister to leave for Ovada and orders her not to send her any food.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to tell you to send Sr. A. Graziosa to Ovada;1 of course it would be better if Fr Antonio could accompany her.2 Meanwhile I am writing to the President; or else, as she has to take the baths, I think she could stay a while in the S. Pier d'Arena house, and so take the baths.3

2. I am sending you the ducklings: 4 for you and 12 for Mamma. Take them to her at once or they will suffer; feed them first.4

3. I forbid you by virtue of holy obedience to send me fish, do you understand? I have orange-flower water to spare. For charity's sake, don't waste money.5

4. Another obedience: I absolutely do not want you to go to the sick. I am sending you this Sr. A. Celeste, who is very dear. For charity's sake, take care of yourself

Goodbye, your Affect. M. R.

She is to take two Sisters to the hospital and hurry the delivery of the beds.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will take Sr. A. Chiara and the one I sent you last, Sr. A. Celeste, to the hospital, and you will take Sr. A. Annunciata,1 at once, as soon as you receive this.

2. I hear they are giving you the beds; now I would like you to tell them I want them for 5 or at the latest 6 June, and earlier if possible.2 Dear daughter, I have a visitation here, and you can imagine how worried I am. I know it is not liked that I leave the beds like this without curtains.3 Try to get them to me.

Goodbye. I am in a hurry, your

Affect. M.

She expresses gratitude for his calling the FSA to his Diocese. She accepts his proposal and asks how to arrange the sending of the Sisters.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. The Reverend Missionary Fr Enrico Tipoli has informed me that Your Most Rev. Excellency wishes to have the poor Daughters of Saint Anne in your City;1 and while thanking you for this kindness towards us, I praise God for inspiring it and accept your proposal, assuring you that we shall do our best to make our feeble work beneficial to your Diocesans.

2. We accept the terms2 Your Most Rev. Excellency offers us, trusting in Divine providence, which will not abandon these poor servants of His, who, blessed by Your Excellency, hope to prove worthy of the kindness you show them.

3. I beg you to tell me by letter how I should arrange to send the sisters there, among whom will be the qualified Teacher you desire.3

4. I hope all will go well, and from this we shall conclude that it is the Lord's will for the poor Daughters of Saint Anne to go there and give their very humble service.

5. Meanwhile we are offering special prayers that the Lord may show us His divine will ever more clearly and enable us to be useful to Your Most Rev. Excellency and act according to your wishes.

6. Your Excellency, send us your pastoral blessing, which will protect us on our journey, with a line to tell me how we should arrange to come, and meanwhile I am sure we shall have our travelling expenses paid.4

Bless the least of all, who remains humbly at your feet

Your most devoted Servant Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

She gladly takes the opportunity to have her letter delivered to him. She is close to him and interested in his business; she has sent him the linen. She encourages him, urging him to look after his health. Carlotta and Gaspare are at Albaro.1

My son,

1. Onorata tells me there is a safe opportunity to send you letters, and I take it at once. Yes, my dear Alessandro, believe that this poor Mother of yours would like an opportunity to write to you every day.

2. I have given the Fr. 40 to the person you told me; just think how I long to hear that you are settled at last, and I am deeply grieved because you are always up in the air, and what is more you are no longer with your cousin.2 Patience!

3. I hope you have received the linen, and the things your uncles sent you to sell, goods and wine. I also saw a magnificent watch.3

4. You see that we all think of you, and it is not true, as you say, that we forget you. No, no! Oh! my God! If you could see how many prayers this poor mother of yours offers, you surely could not entertain the troubling thought that I do not think of you. Oh! My dear Son! One day you will see whether I have thought of you.

5. You ask me about the furniture; your uncles tell me it is not worth it because it costs too much; I sent you the linen at once. I hope you will be able to do something with the goods your uncles sent you.

6. Do not lose heart if something should happen to you on account of your cousin, for you will see that money comes and goes, but the rest, that is health, cannot be recovered. So take care of yourself and remember that everything on this earth comes to an end and only good and evil remain to us, and these two alone we take with us into eternity; good will win us eternal life, and evil, alas! I cannot even think of it, for it would be a grief that would kill me.4 Shall I never see my dear Son again for all eternity? No, Our Lady will keep him good for me and I shall enjoy him for ever.

7. Your sister is still at Albaro with her husband; I assure you that you have gained a true brother, and when you see him you will be pleased.

8. I assure you I have been left in debt on all sides, but with a little economy I hope to recover and be able to satisfy you too by sending you what you ask; but for now you will surely understand.5 Won't you? So be patient, and I hope you will be pleased with what I have done.

Goodbye, dear son; the Father,6 who is here, sends his greetings, and I embrace you, remaining your

affect. M. ROSA GATTORNO

She sends her two letters to deliver in person.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will receive these two letters;1 take one to Advocate Boccardo, you know, Sr. A. Vincenza's uncle, the one who is to handle the Ricchino lawsuit, and the other is for that judge Arrighetti whom you went to see with Sr. A. Benedetta; Fr Accinelli can show you where they live. Take Boccardo the life of Sr. A. Vincenza2 together with the letter, at once, at once. I think I have made myself clear.

Goodbye, courage, and much more in person your most affect. M.R.

She arranges the transfer of two Sisters. She has not yet received everything she asked her to buy.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you have sent Sr. A. Antonina to the new house.1 Listen, for pity's sake, take her out at once and put in Sr. A. ..., the one who had erysipelas, as the air will do her good; and tell her for charity's sake to be good, do the cooking and try to be exemplary; not to behave like a girl, but always be serious and composed, at home and out of doors.

2. Yesterday I sent you a packet with letters inside and also a life of Sr. A. Vincenza to take to her uncle, Advocate Boccardo.2

3. I hope you have understood: this Sister, Sr. A. Antonina,3 you may send to Sestri for a while to take some baths; meanwhile I also enclose a line for the Superior.

Goodbye, your

Affect. M.

4. I have just received the tartan [cloth], but not the pasta; I hope it will arrive.

She asks for permission for Cardinal Berardi to come to the Mother House in Piacenza.

Most Holy Father,

1. As Your Holiness has deigned to grant our poor Institute His Eminence Cardinal Berardi as Protector,1 I make bold to beg Your Holiness that His Eminence may come here to visit the Mother House,2 so that he may see better and become thoroughly imbued with our spirit; and also, for matters of no small importance to the Work, I should like to submit everything to his most wise counsel.

The petitioner, confident of the favour, having kissed the Sacred Foot, prostrates herself with her forehead to the ground

Your Holiness's

Lowliest daughter

Sister A. ROSA GATTORNO

Summons to Piacenza, the Mother House, for the Spiritual Exercises.

A.M.F.

Superior,

1. Having decided that all the Superiors are to make the Holy Exercises at the Mother House in Piacenza, I am giving you too timely notice to arrange your House so that everything runs in order during your absence.1

2. Bring with you the half-yearly accounts for 1876, from 1 January to the end of June.

3. Let me know by letter how many religious with you have completed two and three years of vocation.2

4. The purpose of this Circular is for you to be at this Mother House by the 16th of next month.

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She has received his letter and replies that she cannot send only two Sisters, but three. She awaits his word for their departure.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I have just finished reading your most venerated letter.1 God grant that, according to His will, we may give satisfaction to Your Most Rev. Excellency, who so kindly deigns to welcome us into your Diocese; and I pray most fervently to the Lord that all may turn out for the greater good of souls and the sanctification of those to whom this Mission is given.

2. Your Most Rev. Excellency speaks of only two Sisters,2 and this must surely be because I did not explain myself well enough in the letter I sent you. Two Sisters alone cannot form a community; for Your Excellency's sake I can agree to send just Three, with the [hope] of increasing them later.

3. Your Excellency asks me the name of the Qualified Teacher who will come. She is Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini, qualified for 10 years.

4. As for the Rules, we shall bring them when the sisters come, and when Your Most Rev. Excellency has read them, kindly return them. Meanwhile I send you the purpose of our Institution.3

5. As regards our coming, it will take place when Your Most Rev. Excellency thinks fit and lets me know, and I shall be delighted to send you the sisters.4

Deign to grant your Pastoral blessing to the least Servant of the Lord

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

Her daughter, a Novice in the Institute, wants to go home. She sends her back, explaining the reasons for her return.1

[Dear Madam,]

1. As you will see from your daughter's letter, she absolutely refuses to remain in our Institute any longer, so I must remove her habit and let her return home.

2. Please note that in the two years2 we have had her with us she has always been ill and was no small burden to us, for her illness required much care from doctors, many medicines and very nourishing food; the doctors who treated her can testify [to] this, as can the Paper she herself leaves with us, truthfully attesting what she has received from our poor Institute.

3. Now that she is completely cured she drives us to despair by insisting on leaving and going home, threatening to make a scene if we prevent it. So I am obliged to let her leave for home next Monday.3 Her conduct has always been reprehensible,4 but always excused because of her illness. I believe this is enough without saying more, and I sign myself

Humble Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She invites her to Piacenza for the Superiors' Spiritual Exercises. Directions on founding a new work in Genoa.

A.M.F.

Superior,

1. Having decided that all the Superiors are to make the Holy Exercises at the Mother House in Piacenza,1 I am giving you too timely notice to arrange your House so that all runs in order during your absence.

2. Bring with you the half-yearly accounts for 1876, from 1 January to the end of June.

3. Let me know by letter how many Religious with you have completed two and three years of vocation. These exercises will begin on 16 July.

4. You ask me whom you should appoint as Superior at S. Antonino.2 Sr. A. Elisa provisionally; tell her that after Saint Anne's I shall send her the permanent Superior, as the exercises are on the 16th of that month and it would not be worth her making the journey for so few days.3 You tell me we are to provide the linen; I say no, for I agreed that he must provide everything. Be careful, dear daughter, for otherwise they are all the same, they want to profit at our expense.4

5. The beds have arrived safely and are already set up, as are the chairs, the tartan [cloth] and the lamps.5 Carlotta will not be back for another 5 days; they are both well.

6. As for the other two Sisters, you could take one from Sestri, Sr. A. ..., I don't remember her name, one of the little ones who go begging, a plump one, I think it is Sr. A. Marcellina. If you can manage without them and send them some of your own in Genoa, that will be better,6 all the more so as now, with summer coming, you will not have so many sick. Do as you think best, your

Most affect. M. R. GATTORNO

She complains of her disobedience in continuing to send fish. She sends some ducks by two Sisters, whom she is to place in the community.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. First of all I must complain, because you have not obeyed me by stopping sending fish and certain trifles; now I tell you that I shall send back the first lot I receive, you may be sure of it, except the pasta, which we have already agreed on.1

2. If a few more copies of the Settimana Religiosa2 could be had, you would do me a great favour, as I badly need them; I have received the books, thank you. As for the Sisters you are to send, I told you: for now Sr. A. Elisa,3 and I shall send one from here, who will hand you this letter and will have some ducks for the M.sa Edvige, Sr. A. Benedetta's sister-in-law. Take them to her at once.

3. I am sending you two sisters; one is for S. P. D'Arena: Sr. A. Atanasia will be for S. P. D'Arena and Sr. A. Ampeglia for S. Antonino.4 The latter is well educated, as is the one going to S. P. d'Arena; for the third you will send Sr. A. Faustina, who can do a little cooking and meanwhile rest a bit; I hope she will have come back from the nuns and they will no longer need her.5 If she should still go to them, we shall put in someone else.

4. I am sending you this letter for Ulmi;6 be sure to hand it to him personally, because there is money in it. If need be, you can give it to Fr Accinelli. Goodbye, your

Affect. M. R.

She may send the Sister she wrote about to "S. Antonino".

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have received your letter, and you tell me Sr. A. Faustina is with Mamma.1 Very well, send another, the one you mention; I don't quite remember her, but I hope she will be suitable.

2. Today is the day you go to S. Antonio.2 Let us hope all goes well. I have received the newspapers.3 I hear Mamma is better; I bless God, and let us hope He keeps her well.

Goodbye, your affect. M. R.

She asks her to go to the lawyers to plead the Ricchino case and, if she thinks fit, also to visit the Archbishop.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I enclose two lines to take to the judge you went to see with Sr. A. Benedetta, Signor Arrighetti, and try to plead with him.1 I think you might also go to the others.

2. Listen, what if you went to the Archbishop to tell him you are also at S. Antonio?2 Talk to Fr Antonio first and hear what He says.3 See whether it is a good idea to go or not. I hope you have received Sr. A. Benedetta's letter.

Goodbye, your

Affect. M. R.

She gives instructions about the sisters' profession of vows.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Listen, first of all I tell you to have Sr. A. Fortunata take her vows too; so leave all those of her clothing the order and how they are to make them.1 I am sending you the keys; it was true that I had them here with them.

2. Listen, I won't say more, because we shall see each other soon. I have not yet received the pasta, do you understand? For your guidance.2 Goodbye; did you receive my letter telling you to leave as Superior Sr. A. [Elisa],3 the one who goes begging?

Goodbye, your affect.

M. ROSA

She urges her to go to Advocate Boccardo and the others to discuss the Ricchino case.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received yours and hear what you say about Boccardo; so for charity's sake try to manage to go to all of them1 and take the letter I enclose, to see whether he can be moved.2 You are right that it is a truly strange affair.

2. So take this letter to Advocate Boccardo at once; I leave it open, you will read it and then seal it and take it to him. I say read it so that you see what I tell him and can say the same in person. And don't forget to go to the others.

3. Hurry Fr Antonio, do you understand? Ah! it is just as you say, my dear Daughter, we must get moving! Enough; I strongly commend this matter to you. Goodbye, your

Affect. M. R. G.

Referring to the earlier requests, she points out that a second qualified teacher is inappropriate.

Dear Mr Mayor,

1. I have received your esteemed letter,1 to which I hasten to reply that what was agreed in your first requests2 mentioned only one teacher; so I must regretfully tell you that if Your Lordships now want a second qualified teacher, I could no longer accept the contract, as I do not wish to subject two qualified teachers to so meagre a salary.

2. Kindly reply as soon as possible on this point,3 as I have been called to other places, and so I can arrange things better.4

With distinguished esteem, Your Lordship's

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She expresses gratitude for his choosing the FSA to entrust them with a work in the Diocese. She is ready to negotiate.1

[Most Reverend Excellency,]

1. I have learned from the Rev. Missionary2 that Your Most Rev. Excellency has kindly turned your eyes to this poor Institute of ours, and I thank you and pray God to reward you fittingly. I only regret that I cannot come to arrange the matters concerning the house; so I would ask you to arrange for the person you intend to put in charge3 to come here; otherwise, if that is not possible, I shall send a representative of mine in August.

2. And as I know that Your Most Rev. Excellency often travels to give the Holy Exercises, I would ask you, should you come somewhere nearer Piacenza, to let me know, so that I could come to your feet, as I would rather deal with this matter myself with Your Most Rev. Excellency than through others.

Awaiting a reply,4 prostrate at your feet I ask your pastoral blessing, and remain

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She thanks him for forwarding the Bishop's letter. She has accepted his proposal and will let him know the outcome of the negotiations later.1

Reverend Sir,

1.2 I have received your letter enclosing that of the Bishop of Chioggia, to whom I have replied that I accept the proposal to open a house3 where indicated; but that, as I cannot go to him, I assured him I would send a representative of mine in August; or else, as He often travels to give the Exercises, should he come near Piacenza I asked him to let me know, and I would come in person to his feet to deal with the matter.

2. I shall hear the Bishop's reply and then write to you about it.

3. Father Tornatore sends his greetings, and I, with a thousand thanks for your concern for us, remain yours

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She stresses some aspects of the contract, pointing out the obligations undertaken towards the municipal Administration and her right to transfer and replace the Sisters.

[Dear Mr Mayor,]

1. In reply to your esteemed note of the 3rd inst., I take the liberty of observing that, from the moment you saw fit to entrust the running of your girls' schools and hospital to a Religious Institute, there was no longer any question of invoking the privileges arising from the two articles you cite, whether in favour of the individual teachers or of the Comune.1

2. Yes, I readily understand that a private contract made with an individual is quite a different thing.2

3. The Contract was made with me as Superior General. The individuals working there are my representatives in fulfilling obligations undertaken not by them but by me. In binding myself as Superior to run your schools and hospital, I undertook to keep there persons with the required qualifications, without however binding myself to particular individuals or particular periods as regards their stay, and this for compelling reasons of this Institute.

4. This being so, article 77 invoked in favour of your Comune seems to me out of place. At most I might accept it as valid3 if, regarding what I contracted with you, I wished without reasonable cause to withdraw from the commitment undertaken for your schools and abandon the house without notice; but to claim that I, on whom alone the responsibility towards you rests, may not replace the present teachers with others equally capable, as the Institute requires,4 is to tell me that you are tired of the Daughters of Saint Anne, and to force me without more ado to recall them and withdraw them from that house, so that you may avail yourselves of those who know how and are able to serve you better.

5. Such is the conclusion your stated demands lead me to. And here I end, reserving for another time, if need be, my reply to the second point, concerning the diploma for the infant school, but asking Your Lordship for a line in reply informing me of the decisions your Comune will take following this letter.5

And with due consideration and esteem I remain

Your Lordship's

Humble Servant

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

The Holy Father Pius IX has raised the feast of Saint Anne to a "double of the first class with octave". Sisters making their vows for the first time or renewing them are to apply. The Superiors are to send the names of the Sisters of their communities and of those studying for the teaching qualification.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughters in J. C.,

1. The feast of our Holy Mother, glorious Saint Anne, is approaching. This year her feast has a special feature distinguishing it from previous years: His Holiness Pope Pius IX, gloriously reigning, has raised it for our Institute to a feast of obligation and a Double of the first class with octave.

2. Therefore on the Holy Mother's day we are strictly bound to hear Holy Mass and abstain from all servile work; that is, on that day it is not lawful to work.

3. This is a most distinguished glory with which the Holy Father has honoured our Institute, with the honour given to the greatest Saints of the Church.

4. It is also a new testimony that the Holy Father has honoured our Institute by counting it among the Institutes recognised by the Church.1 We therefore advise the Superiors that on that day they inform the Priests who come to celebrate Holy Mass in our Chapels that for us it is a feast of the first class with octave, so that they know what ceremonies to use.2

5. We also recall that on the feast of the Holy Mother those completing three years of novitiate make their Holy Vows for the first time, and those who have already made them renew them.3 So the former must ask us in good time for leave to make them, and the latter for leave to renew them. On this occasion we also ask the Superiors to send us the first name and surname of every sister in their communities and also the personal number, that is, of the things they have for their use.

Most Illustrious President,

1. It is with the greatest regret that I find myself obliged to send you this letter, the chief purpose of which is to declare that I consider dissolved every agreement between my Institution and the Hospital administration made on [6.6.1876], and this on the basis of facts which would not allow us to continue without prejudice to justice, humanity and morality.

2. Though unwell, I left Piacenza to come to the hospital to verify reports that had reached me there, reports suggesting poor treatment of the sick and no better conduct on the part of the Superior I had placed in charge of the nurses.1 To my great surprise I found myself facing a band of enemies who in concert barred my way, perhaps to prevent me from discovering the truth, which could only convince me that the reports were unfortunately true, though I would gladly have refuted them.

3. Your Lordship was no less harsh in receiving me and, when I asked for another meeting, it was kindly granted for the following day; I could not attend because of my poor health, and when it was postponed I was led to hope for the following Thursday. The Management chose to be no less hostile and likewise took pleasure in hindering my inquiry. Then in recent days I sent sisters of mine to speak with the hospital Sisters, and they were turned away without being able to speak to anyone; and the hospital sisters were prevented from communicating with me. What interpretation should I give to such conduct?

4. I shall say it frankly: collusion2 between Administration, Management and Superior. As for having prevented the Sisters of my Institute from speaking with others from the hospital, it is a fine piece of medieval high-handedness,3 which only the courts could deal with; for my part, meanwhile, I must inform you that the Sisters of my Institute have no bond other than that which ties them to the commitment they make towards humanity to assist, nurse and relieve it; and therefore the pressure, the order given them not to communicate with the others, is an arbitrary act for which no name can be found, and against which I protest strongly in the name of justice.

5. I must stop, not wishing to end in a string of accusations in the form of an indictment; just one last word to urge your Administration warmly to consider this matter as soon as possible, to spare greater harm and settle everything in the most conciliatory way still possible.4

6. I likewise earnestly beg that the ban on

communication between the hospital sisters and those of my other charitable houses be lifted.5

7. As for the manner and time of my sisters' leaving the hospital, it will be agreed jointly, for I certainly do not wish to cause the least harm to the running of the internal administration, which would then harm the poor sick; but I trust provision will be made as soon as possible so that I can withdraw all the sisters.

8. In the hope of seeing this request granted in view of all these unfortunate6 considerations, I have the honour to remain your

[Dearest daughters,]

1. Behold, dearest Daughters, by God's mercy we have entered the new year. Two feelings should be awakened in our hearts: one of gratitude and the other of sorrow; gratitude to our heavenly Father for the many blessings He has poured on our Institute throughout the year now ended. A most remarkable grace, worthy of being mentioned first, is His having given us a new Protector in the Person of His Eminence Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi; from the moment this Cardinal took our Institute under his protection, which was at the very beginning of 1876, he has shown himself a truly loving Father.1

2. He has never ceased to give proofs of fatherly love: a most touching proof was the visit he was pleased to make to our Mother House; he made this visit with His Holiness's consent2 and celebrated the feast of the Holy Mother there. The presence of the Cardinal greatly increased the solemnity of that feast, for it drew a great crowd of distinguished people to venerate the Holy Mother. This visit was a real triumph for our poor Institute. It opened the eyes of many who had paid it no attention; many who had despised it until then changed their contempt into esteem; so this visit was a signal grace the Lord granted us in giving us so great a Protector; and we must pray Him to preserve him for us and enrich him ever more with light and strength for the good of our Institute.

3. What shall we say of the grace the Lord has given us in continuing to the Institute the special goodwill of His Vicar, the Holy Father Pius IX? He showed this special kindness to the Institute by receiving us in audience several times,3 treating us with fatherly cordiality and asking with interest about the Institute's progress.

4. He has a singular affection for our Institute, because our Institute was raised up by the Lord in His Church to honour in a special way that venerable Matron in whose womb the mystery of the Immaculate Conception of Mary was wrought; from the definition of this mystery the Holy Father Pius IX draws that great glory4 by which he shines above all the Popes as the sun outshines the stars.

5. That is why in these early days our Institute has founded and is founding most of its houses in the Pope's state,5 around his Throne, so to speak; for between the Holy Father Pope Pius IX and our Institute there is a secret sympathy, and like a magnet he draws it to himself and wants it to fill his whole state before spreading to other parts of the world; but it is well known that where the Pope's affection goes, there goes the affection of the Bishops and the good faithful.

6. Hence our Lord Bishops, wherever we are, love us and are glad to have us; so too the faithful: they appreciate our services, and very many sick people of every condition ask for our care, both at home and in hospital.

7. Meanwhile, in a hospital which, through the malice of wicked people, we had to leave against our will, although they used every possible means to make us stay, and from which we keep receiving requests to return, the sick weep at no longer having our care, and their tears are joined by those of the good people of that City.6

8. Our schools are very numerous,7 and the Lord blesses them through the Holy Mother's intercession, and the girls make progress there both in virtue and in learning. In this new year, now that we have arranged that in all of them the joy the Holy Mother felt in the Immaculate Conception of Mary be honoured with three Our Fathers, Hail Marys and Glory Bes, which are like the badge distinguishing our schools from those of other Institutes, the blessings will be more abundant.

9. We had a testimony of the affection Bishops and peoples have for us in the year just ended; in it the Institute grew prodigiously both in foundations and in members: we founded nine Houses8 and clothed 76 sisters, and

4 died.

10. See how strong and numerous are the reasons we have, dearest Daughters, to bless and thank the Lord. But have we responded to so many graces? On the whole, by God's grace, the Sisters fulfil the purpose of their vocation, which is to imitate the Holy Mother by keeping the Rules and to honour her prerogatives, especially that of being Mother of the Immaculate; we pay her this honour by reciting at the appointed times the Institute's ejaculatory prayer: blessed be our glorious Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate,9 and reciting it fervently, because it contains a profession of faith by which we believe that Mary, in the womb of our Holy Mother, at the first instant of her conception, was conceived immaculate, that is, without original stain. And since this prayer is almost continuous from morning to night, through it the Institute makes, as it were, a continuous act of faith in the Immaculate Conception of Mary.

11. This imitation of the Holy Mother and this veneration of her prerogatives is the work God wants of us as Daughters of Saint Anne, as a testimony that we love Him. And so it can be said that the Sisters on the whole love the Lord with all their hearts, but it is not true of all that in the past year they were faithful in imitating and venerating the Holy Mother in the way explained.

Dear Sir,

1. I reply by return of post to your esteemed and kind letter. My God! How can I, Your most wretched servant, thank You enough for giving me a new benefactor, so charitable and kind to me, so unworthy a creature!! With what words can I express my gratitude to Your Lordship? I would go on too long if I tried to say what gratitude dictates. I shall only assure you that you will never be forgotten by the poor Daughters of Saint Anne; they will remember you for ever.

2. Here is what has been the rule in the other factories where the Daughters of Saint Anne are.1 The manufacturer binds himself by the year, and the number of years is fixed by mutual agreement; then the number of sisters needed for management, both supervision and teaching, kitchen, housekeeping, all to us, and the linen room.2 As there are many of them, the said sisters' stipend will be set at fr. 300 a year, including firewood and oil both for lighting and cooking.

3. The girls. If the manufacturer wishes to maintain them, food is reckoned at 6.50 a day each,3 and a calculation is made for clothing according to the number: for sixty it is fr. 100 a month;4 the sum increases from there according to the number of girls entrusted to us.

4. These are the points5 of the contract to be made, if Your Lordship finds them to your liking. The other conditions are as in all other contracts: that neither party may terminate except after three years or more, giving

6 months' notice; that this may happen only for just reasons; let the reasons be stated.

5. Enough, I do not wish to add more; Your Lordship will draw up the rest.

6. I only beg, I implore you to send for them as soon as possible, even if they have to be very crowded, because I have received a letter saying the factory closes on 1 May. My God! I don't know where those poor creatures can be put.

7. They have already been without work for a month and6 all their bread has to be paid for; I am tied up here by a thousand matters; I keep writing to beg the charity of devout people to help me. You cannot believe how this thought tears me apart, knowing that they are poor girls all rescued from danger, who are now so good. If they had to go back into danger, what would become of them!!

8. I have placed all my hopes in Mary Most Holy and Saint Anne to protect them. Help me, for pity's sake; send for them without delay, as suits you, in the large and small rooms, [saving them] from the snares of the world.7 This is what I desire; it [is] always a signal grace if you send for them in any way at all.

9. I trust so much in your charity that I shall obtain what I ask, and I beg you to give my respects to your most worthy sister, while I sign myself, full of esteem and gratitude, Your Lordship's

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She describes the character and activity of the Daughters of Saint Anne and commends the Work to their charity.

Most Illustrious Sir,1

1. Eleven years ago there came into being in Piacenza an Institution called the Daughters of Saint Anne, intended to nurse the sick of either sex and every condition free of charge in their own homes. Having grown by a miracle of Providence to number 48 houses, with four in Rome, two of them maintained by His Holiness Pius IX,2 the poor Daughters of Saint Anne wish to inform Your Most Illustrious Lordship that they accept service in public and private Hospitals, the direction of charitable Institutions, not excluding those for the Deaf and Dumb and for the Blind,3 and the instruction and education of girls and also of boys not over eleven years of age.

2. They further wish to make known that they are not bound to other Religious Houses,4 but depend in everything solely on their Mother General, except that, being under the jurisdiction of the respective Bishops, they depend on them chiefly for permission to open new Houses in the towns and places to which they are called.

3. The undersigned therefore warmly commends to the charity of Your Most Illustrious Lordship that you may be pleased to help this pious Work, so that the Daughters of Saint Anne may attain the holy purpose of their institution in your city too.

Affectionate M. R.

She gives precise directions about the boarding school, both as to fees and teachers. She sends a copy of the contract and points out some details about it.1

A.M.F.

My Dearest daughter,

1. I reply to yours;2 I hear you had a reasonable journey; God be blessed for it.

2. Listen, as for the girls, once you have checked [that] the daily expenditure is not greater than the board the Superior receives each month, then let them keep the boarding school; furthermore, if other girls apply, accept them, provided that on top of school, French and piano they pay 5 for French and another 5 francs for piano, which would make 10 fr. more a month.3

3. Sr. A. Ulderica can look after them under Sr. A. Giuseppina's direction,4 and then the teacher for the Italian lesson, and Sr. A. Giuseppina for French and piano. So, as I told you, the latter can act as assistant superior, receive visitors when the Superior is absent, and so on.

4. I am sending you the contract you ask for this very moment.5 As for the schools, we can do as Father Andreotti says and leave him to reorganize them, and that will be very good.6

5. So, dear daughter, courage, for the Lord is with you, and in what you do your good angel will advise you. You will see that all will go well.

6. Listen, I am sending you the account, but you must tell her that while it shows that we paid for the said contract, in fact she did it all, and this was put in for legal reasons;7 likewise certain obligations to pay her a sum, this too was put in for legal reasons; but since she goes on doing as she did before, and so there is nothing between us that is different for her from before, when it was her property, it is the same, she carries on as before.

7. So I close in order to post this soon. Yours affectionately for all ages, my own, my one and only and dearest daughter, who has always relieved and still relieves me in my most painful needs, more than can be said, your

Most affectionate M. R.

She wants to know whether it is true that one day they had nothing to eat but bread and water. She rejoices at the subsidy the Holy Father has given. Advice about the house.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, I want you to tell me the real truth about what I am asking you to tell me frankly. I was told in writing that one day there at the Margana house you had nothing to eat and ate only bread and water; is it true?2

2. I think it is some gossip who has said something; so tell me how matters stand,3 so that I can reply. Listen, towards the middle of the month the Cardinal wants you with him; do go.4

3. I also heard the good news you gave me of the money the Pope has given you. Oh! Great Saint!5 So you did well to buy what you mentioned; now try to arrange things so as to pay for the bread every month; and how is it that the girls do not pay?

4. Listen, the postulant has not yet arrived, because she is in Florence waiting for Sr. A. Benedetta, who is there. Did you give her the wet-nurse's pin?6

5. Goodbye, I am in haste; tell me, has the Bishop written anything about the Postulant you told me about?

your affectionate M. R.

Recommendations about the Florence House and various news. She expects her as soon as possible.1

A.M.F.

My Dearest daughter,

1. Yesterday I wrote to you and registered the letter,2 so you will certainly have received it. I hear from yours that you wrote to Onorata that you are anxious because you have no news; listen, I wrote to you and also sent you the contract; I hope you will have received it all.

2. And listen, you speak of Father Andreotti,3 but you must know that superiors are to be believed only a little;4 first of all observe carefully, and if he says so it is because he is very attached and wants the good of this work; you see it is all zeal? Please bring me the folders he will give you, but for pity's sake don't lose them.

3. I hear you will not be able to sign the contract until Monday, my God! Well, enough! I hope you will soon come back and I shall soon have you with me.

4. If you see that Sr. A. Giuseppina cannot teach, then write to the Father5 and he will see about having her return. Patience!

5. Listen, you will have seen from the telegram Gaspare sent that you are to send the postulant. Enough; I want you to come back soon, so that our mutual worries may be removed,6 because I always fear you overwork. Being alone, you do whatever you like of your own accord, and so you certainly manage somehow; mind, I order you to take care of yourself.

6. Tell Sr. A. Giuseppina that I shall write to her soon; I am so weighed down with work that I do not know which to do first.

7. The Holy Father has given Sr. A. Santina 600 F.;7 she is delighted; now another one in Naples too, except here. Do you know what the ladies have done? Egged on by the Clergy they have refused to pay the annual subsidy they used to give for the boys of the Morte. Oh! what virulence there is, it is truly dreadful.8 Enough, when you return you will hear how, and what an ugly business. Enough, God is with us, and that is enough: whoever has Him has everything.9

8. Goodbye, I am in haste. Your affectionate. Many greetings to good Father An-dreotti; give him my best and ask him to remember his poor mother; and I remain yours for all ages

Affectionate M. R.

She sends the diplomas for the new school about to open. She is glad of her return and expresses gratitude for her kind and timely help.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the diplomas because the telegram does not give the name of the place they are to be sent to properly.2

2. I hear from Father Andreotti's letter that you will arrive here tomorrow; God grant it! So I shall tell you everything in person.

3. Oh yes, my beneficent Angel that you have been, the only one who knew how to get me out of such sad troubles, out of my d...3 Enough, may God the Eternal Father, my Only One on earth and in Heaven, make you a true vessel of his election, as I already know you are among the number of the predestined!

4. Alas! What am I saying, where am I going now? Burn this letter at once and remember that you are always present to me, or rather at my side.

Goodbye, yours for all ages

Affectionate M. Sr. A. R.

5. The post is leaving; yours. The certificates4 I shall send under wrapper. Goodbye. Do not stop at Bologna, you will hear why in person; don't stay; going to the... C.5

She should ask the Mayor whether he can accept a Sister who has only a certificate in place of the diploma. The rule is suitable for that boarding school.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to tell you that I have received yours and am glad to hear that you are already starting the school, that is, the boarding school.2

2. Listen, if the Mayor of Maratea were agreeable I would send him one with a certificate, who failed the diploma by two points but can quite well teach,3 you know, like you when you had to resit a subject.

3. If he wants her, let him telegraph me at once; if not, I shall send her elsewhere, where they would already be waiting for her; so press for an answer at once.

4. Listen, I have also received the paper, that is, the rule.4 It is fine for your house, but it certainly cannot be general; I think the one I sent you [a copy of] is much better and more fully explained;5 I understand it is meant for internal use, so all is well.

Goodbye, I hold you close in my Crucified One and remain your affectionate M. R.

She urges her to have the dowry coupons of a Roman Sister cashed. She asks for some items for the raffle. She charges her with speaking to Cardinal Berardi on the occasion of the outing.1

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Listen, by tomorrow I shall send you the certificates of those Sisters in Rome so as to collect the money from the Congregation2 which you said their relatives have. It would be better for you to get them handed over, then Father Agostino would check them and so it would be quicker; or do you know who would do it well for me, to get them soon? Father Fulgenzio of the little Parish. He is quick; then the money would serve you for the rent, which is almost due. So see about it; I shall send you the certificates, but this friar does things so well and will tell you better how to proceed; get them to give you the papers of Father Sempliciano's girl; it looks like quite a muddle to me.3

2. Listen, see whether you can find me some nice items for a raffle I am organizing for the little boys of the Morte,4 and when there is an opportunity send them to me.

3. Now I hear you are going to the Cardinal;5 tell him you would like to know who that wicked tongue was who said you had eaten only bread and water, which is not true, and then the sisters can say so.6 I have written to him7 that you have the books, for the meat, the bread and the grocer, because when I was in Rome I had them. Well, you will hear.

Goodbye, your

affectionate M. R.

She approves the rebuke given to a Sister for spreading untrue news that put "the Superiors" in a bad light.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. I receive your dear letter and am truly glad to hear that you gave that proud one a piece of your mind: well done!2 So it is right that you spoke firmly to S...3 Yes, firmly, and he must put a stop to it, because it is a real scandal for Superiors to be trampled underfoot; it is time to put an end to it.4 Take courage and speak firmly.

2. As for her, you must sing it to her in music, for with God's help the truth will shine out, and she, the liar, will surely be thoroughly humiliated. Goodbye, yours in my dear Crucified One

Affectionate M. R.

She reassures him about the arrival of the two Sisters. She invokes blessings on his good work and thanks him.

Most Reverend Canon,

1. My poor health did not allow me to answer your most esteemed letter of the 23rd inst. at once;1 I do so this evening through another pen,2 being unable to do it myself for the same reason. Your kindness will receive it as I send it, for your reassurance about the Sisters' arrival.3

2. I hope no obstacle will prevent them from being there on the day we agreed in my letter. But since there may be delays in the Sisters' arrivals or departures and they might not arrive on the appointed day, do not be concerned. I say this for your greater peace of mind.

3. May the Lord bless your work in your Town,4 so that it may bear abundant fruit for the salvation of souls.

4. May the Lord and Saint Anne bless you and your holy intentions, while this poor creature thanks the good God for so many consolations.

Please accept my respectful regards, while, humbled at your feet, I remain, Most Reverend Canon,

Your most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She speaks of the transfer of some Sisters and of Sr. A. Agnese Sismondini. Instructions about withdrawing the Sisters from the Tor de' Specchi house.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am writing in my own hand although I am unwell. Listen, as soon as you receive this, send Sr. A. Aprotasina at once to Foligno with another Sister you can spare.2 She really needs to be in place by the vigil of All Saints, otherwise it is a serious matter, my God! Quickly, for pity's sake!

2. I have received all your letters and you will already have ours, which Sr. A. Agnese will have brought you.3 Ah yes, she is really capable; I commend her to you. She plays well and works well, speaks French, English and Spanish; in short, it is a real pity to have to send her to so few girls.4

3. As for the Sisters you say you have sent to Mon-talto, Sr. A. Felice certainly seems to me too young for that place, where there are so many men. Well, since I shall have to take some to put in another house, everything will be sorted out; the other one is fine.5 Goodbye,

your Affectionate M. R.

4. Please remove everything,6 the chapel and the rest; the kitchen things belong to the ladies, the rest is ours; I don't remember about the beds, but I think they are ours; you can ask the older ones, such as Sr. A. Crocifissa.7

5. Many greetings to Father Agostino.

6. For the moment, while Tor de' Specchi is about to close,

you can put Illuminata there.8 I have already written that I cannot accept the rooms, that it is impossible to do so; for pity's sake, in case they gave you notice to quit.9

She thanks them for the handiwork sent to her, blesses them and asks prayers for Alessandro.

My daughter,

1. A line to tell you that I have received the little box with the handiwork inside.1 Thank you all so very much. They are excellent and you have done everything well.

2. I rejoice to hear you are well and good. Oh! the goodness of the Lord! God bless you and make you saints, great saints.

3. Pray for my Alessandro, that God may make him a saint too.2 Goodbye, greetings to you all, and believe me ever your

Affectionate M. ROSA
